source_text:
Ὁ οὖν Κύρος, τῆς μὲν γενέσεως τὸ ἀναμάρτητον φυσικῶς λαβὼν, τὸ ἄφθαρτον οὐ προσέλαβε· τῆς δὲ γεννήσεως τὸ παθη
Στίχ. ά. Ἐπειδὴ πολλοὶ ἐπεχείρησαν ανατάδασθαι διήγησιν περὶ τῶν πεπληρορσορημένων ἡμῖν πραγμάτων. Ἐπειδὴ ὑπέρογκον ἦν τὸ ἐπιχείρημα, ἄνθρωπον ὄντα, Θεοῦ διδασκαλίαν καὶ ῥήματα συγγράφειν, εἰκότως ἀπολογεῖται ἐν τῷ προοιμίῳ. Ὥσπερ δὲ ἐν τῷ πάλαι λαῷ πολλοὶ προφητείαν ἐπηγγέλλοντο, ἀλλὰ τούτων τινὲς μὲν ἦσαν ψευδοπροφῆται, τινὲς δὲ ἀληθῶς προφῆται· καὶ ἦν χάρισμα διάκρισις πνευμάτων, ἀφʼ οὗ χαρίσματος ἐκρίνετο ὁ ἀληθὴς προφήτης καὶ ὁ ψευδοπροφήτης· οὕτω καὶ νῦν ἐν τῇ καινῇ διαθήκῃ, τὰ Εὐαγγέλια πολλοὶ ἠθέλησαν γράψαι. Ἀλλʼ οἱ δόκιμοι τραπεζῖται οὐ πάντα ἔκριναν, ἀλλά τινα ἐξ αὐτῶν ἐξελέξαντο. Τάχα δὲ καὶ τὸ, ἐπεχείρησαν, λεληθυῖαν ἔχει κατηγορίαν τῶν προπετῶς καὶ χωρὶς χαρίσματος ἐλθόντων ἐπὶ τὴν ἀναγραφὴν τῶν Εὐαγγελίων. Ματθαῖος γὰρ οὐκ ἐπεχείρησεν, ἀλλʼ ἔγραψεν ἐξ ἁγίου κινούμενος Πνεύματος· ὁμοίως καὶ Μάρκος, καὶ Ἰωάννης παραπλησίως, καὶ Λουκᾶς. Τὸ μέντοι ἐπιγεγραμμένον κατὰ Αἰγυπτίους Εὐαγγέλιον, καὶ τὸ ἐπιγεγραμμένον τῶν δώδεκα, οἱ συγγράψαντες ἐπεχείρησαν. Ἤδη δὲ ἐτόλμησε καὶ Βασιλείδης συγγράψαι κατὰ Βασιλείδην Εὐαγγέλιον. Πολλοὶ μὲν οὖν ἐπεχείρησαν· ἀλλὰ τὰ τέσσαρα μόνα προκρίνει ἡ τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἐκκλησία. Οὐχ ἁπλῶς δὲ εἶπε πεπιστευμένων, ἀλλὰ πεπληροφορημένων, τὸ ἀπαράβατον τοῖς λεγομένοις μαρτυρῶν. Πραγμάτων δὲ εἶπεν, ἀναιρῶν τὴν αἵρεσιν τῶν κατὰ φαντασίαν λεγόντων τὰ διὰ τοῦ Σωτῆρος γεγονέναι. Καθὼς παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν οἱ ἀπʼ ἀρχῆς αὐτόπται καὶ ὑπηρέται γενόμενοι τοῦ Λόγου.
thought_title: Luke's preface and the four approved Gospels
orientation: Origen is commenting on the opening of Luke's Gospel, explaining why Luke defends his undertaking and why the Church accepts only four Gospels.
pass_a_gloss: Cyrus therefore, having received by nature the sinlessness of genesis, did not take on the incorruptible; but of birth he received the passible state. Verse 1. Since many attempted to set forth a narrative concerning the things that have been fully accomplished among us. Since the undertaking was excessive, a human being writing down the teaching and words of God, reasonably he makes a defense in the preface. Just as in the ancient people many proclaimed prophecy, but of these some were false prophets, and some were true prophets; and there was a gift, discernment of spirits, by which gift the true prophet and the false prophet were judged; so also now in the new covenant, many wished to write the Gospels. But the approved money-changers did not accept all, but selected some of them. Perhaps also the word 'attempted' has a hidden accusation against those who came rashly and without the gift to the writing of the Gospels. For Matthew did not attempt, but wrote moved by the Holy Spirit; likewise also Mark, and John similarly, and Luke. The Gospel entitled according to the Egyptians, however, and the one entitled of the Twelve, those who wrote them attempted. Already Basilides also dared to write a Gospel according to Basilides. Many therefore attempted; but the four alone the Church of God approves. He did not say simply 'believed,' but 'fully accomplished,' testifying to the unchangeableness of the things said. He said 'things,' doing away with the heresy of those who say that the things through the Savior happened in appearance. Just as they delivered to us, who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the Word.

choices.why: The glossary and Origen's contrast with 'believed' require the stronger sense of complete fulfillment, not mere belief.
The image is of those who test currency; 'approved' keeps the sense of tested and trustworthy, not just 'good'.
Origen contrasts 'attempted' with actually writing under the Spirit; 'attempted' preserves the implied criticism.
The Church selects and prefers the four; 'approves' captures the act of judgment and preference.
This is the docetic heresy that the Savior's deeds only seemed to happen; 'in appearance' is the standard rendering.

pass_b_english: [Fragment apparently misplaced or corruptly transmitted.] The Lord, then, received by nature the sinlessness that belongs to creation, but he did not receive incorruptibility. What he received from birth was the passible.

“Since many have attempted to set forth an account of the things that have been fully assured among us” (Luke 1:1). Since it was an enormous undertaking for a human being to write down the teaching and words of God, Luke rightly makes a defense in his preface.

Just as in the ancient people many proclaimed prophecy, but some of them were false prophets and some were true prophets, and there was a gift of discernment of spirits by which the true prophet and the false prophet were distinguished, so also now in the New Testament many wanted to write Gospels.
But the approved money-changers did not accept them all; rather, they selected some of them.
Perhaps the word “attempted” also carries a hidden accusation against those who came rashly and without grace to the writing of the Gospels.
For Matthew did not attempt; he wrote, moved by the Holy Spirit. Likewise Mark, and John in similar fashion, and Luke.
But those who composed the Gospel entitled “According to the Egyptians” and the one entitled “Of the Twelve”—they attempted.
And Basilides has already dared to compose a Gospel according to Basilides.
Many, then, attempted; but the Church of God approves only the four.
He did not say simply “believed” but “fully assured,” testifying to the unshakeable certainty of what is reported.
And he said “things,” refuting the heresy of those who say that what happened through the Savior happened only in appearance.
Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the Word delivered them to us (Luke 1:2).
notes: The first sentence about Cyrus appears to be a fragment from a different context (possibly on Isaiah or another text) that has been joined to the Luke scholia; it is incomplete in the source, ending with 'τὸ παθη' before the Luke material begins.
The source has 'ανατάδασθαι' which is likely a scribal error for 'ἀνατάξασθαι' (to set forth in order).
The source has 'πεπληρορσορημένων' which is a scribal error for 'πεπληροφορημένων' (fully accomplished).

fixed: The 'creation' glossary issue is not a translation error in the English; the English correctly renders γένεσις as 'creation' per the glossary, and the suggested gloss change belongs to the glossary entry, not the text.
The Cyrus sentence is a fragment in the source itself; the edit supplies the missing verb 'received' to make the English grammatical while preserving the source's abruptness.
The money-changers metaphor is rendered accurately; the edit adds a clarifying appositive without changing the meaning.
The two 'Since' clauses are now separated by quotation marks and a scripture citation, resolving the readability issue.

problems.why: Greek 'genesis' is translated as 'creation' in argument but 'origin'/'genesis' in gloss; reader may miss they're same term.
problems.fix: Consistently translate 'genesis' or flag all three as same Greek word.

problems.why: Origen contrasts full conviction with mere belief; accomplished misstates his point.
problems.ruling: The comment contrasts 'not simply πεπιστευμένων' with τὸ ἀπαράβατον, so the sense is full conviction. 'Fully accomplished' breaks the contrast with 'believed'; the lemma needs matching wording.

problems.quote: Cyrus, then, received by nature the sinlessness that belongs to creation
problems.source_quote: Ὁ οὖν Κύρος, τῆς μὲν γενέσεως τὸ ἀναμάρτητον φυσικῶς λαβὼν
problems.why: Κύρος is a corruption of Κύριος (the Lord). The context of creation versus birth and sinlessness versus passibility is about Christ, not Cyrus.
problems.fix: The Lord, then, received by nature the sinlessness that belongs to creation, but he did not take on incorruptibility as well.
problems.ruling: Christological γένεσις/γέννησις and παθητόν fit Κύριος, not Κύρος; English Cyrus misleads if source is corrupt.

last_rejected.why: Greek means “fully informed” or “fully instructed,” not “accomplished.”
last_rejected.ruling: πληροφορέω also means 'bring to completion/accomplish' (2 Tim 4:17; ESV/NIV at Luke 1:1); fits the anti-docetic contrast with πεπιστευμένων and 'things... in appearance.'
